'''''Liquidambar formosana''''', commonly known as the '''Formosan gum''', '''Chinese sweet gum''' and '''Formosa sweet gum''',<ref name="hance"/> is a species of tree in the family [[Altingiaceae]] native to East and Southeast Asia.

==Description==
''Liquidambar formosana'' is a large deciduous tree that grows up to 30-40m tall. The leaves are 10~15 cm wide,<ref name="hora" /> and are three-lobed unlike five- to seven-lobed leaves of most American ''Liquidambar'' species.<ref>{{cite book|last=Straley|first=Gerald|title=Trees of Vancouver: A Guide to the Common and Unusual Trees of the City|year=1992|publisher=University of British Columbus Press|pages=128}}</ref> The foliage of the ''L. formosana'' turns a very attractive red color in autumn.<ref name="conserv">{{cite web|title=Tree Conservation|url=http://www.conservancy.org.hk/educate/trees/treedata/page_2E.htm|accessdate=26 April 2012|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20141008185525/http://www.conservancy.org.hk/educate/Trees/treedata/page_2E.htm|archivedate=8 October 2014}}</ref> Leaves grow in an alternate arrangement, and are simple, [[palmate]]ly-veined, with serrated margins. Roots can be aggressive and branches are usually covered with corky projections. The individual flowers of ''L. formosana'' are unisexual. However, both sexes can be found in the same plant ([[Monoecy|monoecious]]).<ref>{{cite web|last=Jackes|first=Bethsy|title=Liquidambar formosana|url=https://www.jcu.edu.au/discover-nature-at-jcu/plants/plants-on-townsville-campus2/liquidambar-formosana|publisher=James Cook University|accessdate=2 April 2016}}</ref> Male flowers are in [[catkin]]s, female flowers form dense spherical heads, and the fruit is burr-like because of the persistent [[Style (botany)|style]]s.<ref name="conserv" />

==Distribution and habitat==
''Liquidambar formosana'' grows mostly in woodland in warm temperate zones. It requires moist soil and can grow in light to no shade areas.<ref name= "hance">{{cite web|title=Liquidambar formosana-Hance|url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Liquidambar+formosana|publisher=Plants for a Future|accessdate=26 April 2012}}</ref>  It is found in Hong Kong, Central and Southern China, South Korea, Taiwan, Laos and Vietnam.<ref name="hora">{{cite book|last=Hora|first=Bayard|title=The Oxford Encyclopedia of the Trees of the World|url=https://archive.org/details/oxfordencycloped00hora|url-access=registration|year=1981|publisher=Oxford University PRess|pages=[https://archive.org/details/oxfordencycloped00hora/page/182 182], 183|isbn=978-0-19-217712-4 }}</ref>

==Uses==

===Medicinal===
''Liquidambar formosana'' has many medicinal uses.  The leaves and roots are used in the treatment of cancerous growths. The stem bark is used in the treatment of fluxes and skin diseases. The fruits used in the treatment of arthritis, lumbago, oedema, oliguria, and decreased milk production and skin diseases. The resin from the stems is used to treat bleeding boils, carbuncles, toothache and tuberculosis. The trunk of this tree can be used for aromatic resin.<ref name= "hance" /> The extract of this resin is used to promote blood circulation and relieve pain.

===Other uses===
''Liquidambar formosana'' is rare in cultivation but in its native regions the wood is used for making tea chests and the leaves to feed silk worms.<ref name="hora" />
